newsitem.title: JAPAN: India headed for place among top economies - Goldman.
newsitem.headline: India headed for place among top economies - Goldman.

text.p: India has good potential for growth and is eventually heading for a place among strong world economies, although this will take time, Robert Hormats, vice chairman of U.S. brokerage Goldman Sachs (International), said on Thursday.
"All the fundamentals are there. India has the potential to be a major player in the global economy," Hormats told Reuters.

Hormats was in Tokyo to attend a two-day meeting of the India Development Forum that began on Thursday, comprising aid agencies led by the World Bank, western donor nations, Japan and leading fund providers such as investment banks.
It is the first time the forum has met in Asia, which Hormats said is in response to investors' shifting interests.

"There is a major and quite significant change...a growing feeling that Japanese investors are widening their interest," he said, although he noted that many concerns remain, such as inadequate infrastructure.

"The government itself understands that it needs investment in infrastructure, because if it doesn't get this, it's going to be much harder to raise the living standards...So I think the government is going to be quite attentive to the concerns of the foreign investor who wants to put money into India."

Officials in India said last week that the government's top priority was infrastructure development, with the second day of the Tokyo meeting aimed at attracting investors into projects related to power, transport, telecommunications and water supply.
On the plus side, Hormats said, India has a well-educated population, a long-established legal system, business people with international experience, and is a democracy.
Given this, he added: "I suspect that for some Japanese companies looking to broaden their exposure in Asia, the low wage and low cost investment is likely to be quite attractive."

Hormats said that India does have some image problems, particularly after protests blocked work on a power plant by U.S. energy giant Enron for almost a year and forced Kentucky Fried Chicken to suspend operations, but said the resolution of the Enron case "has probably smoothed roads out for those who come after...Many foreign companies are doing quite well."
He added that Goldman Sachs has committed about $100 million in direct investments of its own.
